paragraphs.text: This leaf comes from [Banzhang](banzhang:where-it-is), a group of tea villages on Bulang Mountain in the south of Menghai County, Xishuangbanna. The name covers more than one settlement. Lao Banzhang is the old village, and [Xin Banzhang](banzhang:old-and-new) was founded by people who moved out of it. The old village's tea sells for far more.

It is [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from 1980, kept loose rather than pressed. Raw pu’er begins as [maocha](sheng:making), the sun-dried rough tea, and is never put through shou’s fast fermentation, so it changes slowly in [storage](sheng:aging), and the store it was kept in is part of its history. After forty-six years it is well past the ten or twenty years the trade counts as [aged](sheng:ageing).

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
